title: Conditional Expectation
short: E[X ∣ Y = y] averages X within one slice, and E[X] = E[E[X ∣ Y]] averages the slices.
trouble: Students average the conditional means without weighting them by the probabilities of the slices.

blocks.html: The law of total probability finds a probability by splitting into cases. The same idea works for averages: find the average within each case, then average those, weighting each case by its probability. Within a case the average comes from the conditional distribution.

$$E[X \mid Y = y] = \sum_x x\,P(X = x \mid Y = y)$$ is the mean of $X$ within the slice $Y = y$. The tower rule: $$E[X] = \sum_y E[X \mid Y = y]\,P(Y = y),$$ written compactly as $E[X] = E\left[E[X \mid Y]\right]$.

Start from $E[X] = \sum_{x, y} x\,p(x, y)$ and write each cell as $$p(x, y) = P(X = x \mid Y = y)P(Y = y)$$ Grouping by $y$: $$E[X] = \sum_y P(Y = y)\sum_x x\,P(X = x \mid Y = y) = \sum_y P(Y = y)\,E[X \mid Y = y].$$ So $E[X]$ is a weighted average of the slice means, with the slice probabilities as weights.

blocks.cap: Each row with its own mean of X in the last column. Weighting those row means by the row totals gives the overall mean of X.

blocks.title: Slice means from a table
blocks.q: From the table, find $E[X \mid Y = 0]$, $E[X \mid Y = 1]$ and $E[X]$.

blocks.title: A two-stage experiment
blocks.q: Roll a fair die to get $N$, then flip a fair coin $N$ times. Find the expected number of heads.
steps: Given $N = n$, the heads are binomial with mean $\frac{n}{2}$: $E[X \mid N] = \frac{N}{2}$.

blocks.title: Group averages
blocks.q: A school's students: 50% in group 1 with mean commute 30 minutes, 30% in group 2 with mean 40, 20% in group 3 with mean 60. Find the mean commute overall.
steps: The plain average of the three means, about 43.3, is wrong: group 3 is small.

blocks.html: Averaging the conditional means without weighting them by the probabilities of their slices. Check: the overall mean must lie between the smallest and largest slice means, closer to the big slices; and it must agree with $E[X]$ computed from the marginal distribution.
